description: Mizan is a team taking on “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” We’re building a tool that tests whether changes in NASA climate data are real or just noise, starting with Saudi Arabia: heat, rain, groundwater and the Red Sea.
summary:
Mizan (Arabic for “balance”) is a web app that weighs the evidence in NASA data before calling a change a trend. Pick a place, a variable and a season, and Mizan shows how it has changed since 1981, how fast it is changing per decade, and a verdict with its reasons: Robust, Inconclusive or Abrupt shift.

The challenge asks what is changing, where, by how much, and whether it is statistically significant. Mizan answers each one using NASA POWER data. It checks the record length, looks for a single abrupt step, tests the rest against noise with a correction for neighbouring years, tests the sunlight record’s 2001 change of source, and repeats the test across every start and end year.

Across 525 tests for 15 areas of Saudi Arabia, a plain trend line calls 319 significant; Mizan confirms 207 and explains why it does not confirm the other 112. On simulated noise, a plain line raises false alarms up to 44% of the time; Mizan stays near 5%.

A rising line is easy to draw and easy to misread. Mizan helps journalists, teachers, students and planners tell real change from noise.
details:
What it does
Mizan (Arabic for “balance”) checks whether a change in NASA data is a real trend. Pick a place, a variable and a season. Mizan shows how the value changed since 1981, how fast it is changing per decade with a 95% range, and one of three verdicts with its reasons: Robust, Inconclusive or Abrupt shift.

How it works
Every record goes through the same checks:

  1. Record length: at least 20 complete years.
  2. Shift and noise test: Mizan first checks whether one abrupt step explains the record better than a line. It then runs a Mann-Kendall test, measuring the noise around any step and correcting for neighbouring years that resemble each other. For sunlight, it also checks whether NASA POWER’s 2001 change of data source explains the change.
  3. Size: a Theil-Sen slope whose 95% range must exclude zero.
  4. Stress test: the test is repeated for every start and end year, and 90% of periods of 20+ years must agree.

Where several places are tested together, p-values are corrected for testing many places at once (Benjamini-Hochberg).

What we found
Across 525 tests (15 areas × 7 variables × 5 seasons), an ordinary trend line calls 319 significant. Mizan confirms 207 (190 Robust, 17 Abrupt shift) and disagrees on 112: 47 fail the noise test, 30 fail the stress test, 34 do not survive the correction for testing many places, and 1 is explained by the 2001 sunlight switch. Yearly air temperature rises in all 15 areas, by 0.24 to 0.49 °C per decade. Our clearest trap: winter sunlight in Dammam, where a plain line reports p = 0.003, but the change matches NASA POWER’s 2001 switch from GEWEX SRB to CERES. An open question: 11 of the 17 abrupt shifts fall in 1998–99.

Is it reliable?
We tested Mizan on 17 kinds of simulated record where the truth is known. On pure noise, a plain line raises false alarms up to 44% of the time; Mizan stays near 5%. The trade-offs: Mizan confirms only about a third of weak trends, often reads a step as a gradual trend, and trimming 2 years from either end of the record changes 9% of verdicts.

Benefits and impact
Journalists, teachers, students and planners can check a claim about a changing climate without a statistics degree. Every verdict explains itself, and “Inconclusive” is clearly different from “nothing is changing”.

Tools
Python, Streamlit, Plotly, pandas, NumPy and SciPy, hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud. Data comes from the NASA POWER monthly API. The built-in areas use saved copies, so the app works even if the API is down. The code is open on GitHub with automated tests.

What we considered
Each value covers a grid cell, about 55 km for weather and 110 km for sunlight, not a single city. Desert rainfall is unreliable. A robust trend says that something changed, not why.
